title: Eat currywurst standing up at a Berlin Imbiss
description: Invented by Herta Heuwer in 1949 from ration-shop ketchup and curry powder. Konnopke's has been under the U-Bahn viaduct since 1930.

title: Order a doner the way Berlin invented it
description: The doner in bread was a Berlin invention in the 1970s, not a Turkish one. Salad, sauce and grilled vegetables, which is the local difference.

title: Cycle the Schladitzer See and stop for a currywurst at Wolteritz
description: An open-cast lignite mine flooded into a lake north of Leipzig, with a flat ring road right around it. The beach cafe at Dorfstrasse 25, 04435 Schkeuditz does the currywurst you have earned by then.

title: Eat weisswurst before noon, as the rule demands
description: Made fresh each morning without preservatives, so tradition says they must not hear the midday bell. Sweet mustard, a pretzel, and you suck them out of the skin.

title: Buy a Dresdner Stollen at the Christmas market
description: Germany's oldest Christmas market, running since 1434, and the only place the protected Dresden stollen is sold by the people who bake it.

title: Drink Kolsch from a 200ml Stange until you say stop
description: The Kobes keeps replacing your small glass and marking your beer mat. Put the mat on top of the glass when you have had enough.

title: Eat a Thuringer Rostbratwurst off a charcoal grill
description: Protected by origin, at least 15cm long, and grilled over charcoal with mustard in a roll that is deliberately too small for it.

title: Eat a Fischbrotchen on the harbour
description: Pickled herring, onion and remoulade in a bread roll, eaten by the water. The northern answer to a sausage.

title: Eat a proper Wiener schnitzel, veal and hammered thin
description: If it is pork it is legally a schnitzel Wiener Art, not a Wiener schnitzel. Figlmuller's is pork and the size of the plate; Vienna forgives it.

title: Share a Salzburger Nockerl
description: Three baked peaks of sweetened egg white meant to look like the hills around the city. Made to order and collapses within minutes.

title: Scrape raclette off the wheel
description: Half a wheel of cheese held to the heat and scraped onto potatoes, gherkins and pickled onions. Winter food, and the Valais does it properly.

title: Eat Zurcher Geschnetzeltes with rosti
description: Veal in a cream and white wine sauce with a potato cake beside it, and the one dish the city claims outright.

title: Work through a Trappist beer list
description: Only a handful of breweries anywhere may call themselves Trappist and six of them are Belgian. Westvleteren is sold at the abbey gate by appointment.

title: Eat moules-frites in season
description: Mussels come from the Netherlands, the recipe is Belgian, and the season runs when there is an R in the month.

title: Eat raw herring the Dutch way, held by the tail
description: Hollandse Nieuwe lands in June, brined lightly and served with onion and pickle. Tip your head back and lower it in.

title: Order bitterballen with your beer
description: Crumbed balls of beef ragout, molten inside, served with mustard. The standard Dutch answer to a drink before dinner.

title: Eat bacalhau, one of the several hundred ways
description: Salt cod, imported from the Atlantic since the 1500s, and the country will tell you there is a recipe for every day of the year.

title: Take on a francesinha
description: Steak, sausage and ham between bread, buried in melted cheese and a beer-and-tomato sauce, with an egg and chips. One is a whole day.

title: Eat a full Irish with white and black pudding
description: Rashers, sausage, both puddings, egg, tomato and soda bread. The puddings are the part visitors skip and should not.

title: Eat Galway oysters straight from the bay
description: Native flat oysters, in season only when there is an R in the month, with a festival every September since 1954.

title: Eat pie and mash with liquor and jellied eels
description: A working London food older than fish and chips, down to a handful of shops. The green liquor is parsley sauce, not gravy.

title: Eat fish and chips at a proper seaside chippy
description: Fried in beef dripping in the north, cooked to order, salt and vinegar, eaten out of paper looking at the harbour.

title: Eat haggis, neeps and tatties
description: Sheep offal, oats and pepper in a casing. It is much better than its reputation, and there is a vegetarian version everywhere.

title: Try laverbread and cockles at Swansea market
description: Boiled seaweed rolled in oats and fried with bacon. Welsh breakfast, and an acquired taste worth acquiring.

title: Eat a canele fresh from the oven
description: Burnt-caramel crust, custard middle, baked in copper moulds lined with beeswax. Stale within hours, so buy them warm.

title: Eat bouillabaisse where the fishermen made it
description: Broth first with rouille and croutons, then the fish. A charter sets which species must be in it; anything cheap is not the real thing.

title: See a wheel of parmigiano cracked open
description: Dairies open for morning visits, and the wheels are tapped with a hammer to hear whether they have aged evenly.

title: Eat a cannolo filled to order
description: Sheep's-milk ricotta piped in as you order. Filled in advance the shell goes soft, and Sicilians will tell you so.

title: Eat paella where it comes from, at lunchtime
description: Rabbit, chicken and beans over wood, no chorizo, cooked at midday beside the rice paddies of the Albufera lagoon.

title: Eat fabada in an Asturian sidreria
description: White beans with chorizo, morcilla and pork belly. One bowl is lunch and most of the afternoon.

title: Eat souvlaki from a pita stand after midnight
description: Pork, tomato, onion, tzatziki and chips inside the pita, wrapped in paper. Ask for it apo ola and you get the lot.

title: Eat a Cretan dakos and drink raki with it
description: Barley rusk soaked in tomato with mizithra cheese, and the raki that arrives free at the end of every Cretan meal.

title: Eat pierogi at a milk bar
description: Bar mleczny are subsidised canteens left over from the communist era, still cheap and still serving the same dumplings.

title: Eat svickova with bread dumplings
description: Beef in a root vegetable cream sauce with cranberry and a spoon of whipped cream. The national dish, and rarely on tourist menus.

title: Eat goulash as the soup it actually is
description: Gulyas is a thin paprika soup, not the stew served abroad. The stew you are thinking of is porkolt.

title: Eat fuzi with truffle in Istria
description: Hand-rolled pasta with shaved truffle from the Motovun forest, in the Italian-influenced north-west.

title: Take a fika seriously
description: Coffee and a cardamom bun, sitting down, not at a desk. It is closer to an institution than a snack.

title: Eat fresh brown crab on the Bergen fish market
description: Landed that morning and dressed in front of you, on a quay that has traded fish since the 1200s.

title: Eat smorrebrod at lunchtime with a beer and a snaps
description: Open rye sandwiches, eaten in a set order from fish to meat to cheese. A lunch dish only, never dinner.

title: Eat a Karelian pie with egg butter
description: Rye crust around rice porridge, topped with butter mashed into boiled egg. Sold in every supermarket and eaten daily.

title: Eat an Icelandic hot dog with everything on it
description: Lamb in the sausage, crispy onions underneath, remoulade on top. Ask for eina med ollu and join the queue.

title: Eat sarmale with mamaliga and sour cream
description: Cabbage rolls stuffed with pork and rice, slow-cooked for hours, with polenta. Every family insists on their own version.

title: Eat banitsa for breakfast with ayran
description: Filo layered with white cheese and egg, sold hot from bakeries before work, with a salty yoghurt drink.

title: Eat cevapi with kajmak and onion
description: Small grilled minced-meat rolls in flatbread, with a clotted dairy spread the whole Balkans argues over.

title: Eat a balik ekmek off a boat at Eminonu
description: Grilled mackerel in bread, sold from boats rocking at the quay under Galata Bridge, with onion and lemon.

title: Sit at a ramen counter and order from the machine
description: You buy a ticket from a vending machine at the door and hand it over. Regional styles differ completely: tonkotsu, shoyu, miso, shio.

title: Eat okonomiyaki cooked on the counter in front of you
description: Cabbage batter cooked on a hotplate with whatever you choose in it. Osaka mixes it; Hiroshima layers it and adds noodles.

title: Eat yudofu at a temple restaurant
description: Simmered tofu in kombu broth, developed by Zen monks who ate no meat. Kyoto's soft water is the reason its tofu is famous.

title: Eat boat noodles by the bowl until you stack them
description: Tiny intensely spiced bowls, once sold from canal boats. You keep ordering and the empties pile up as the bill.

title: Eat khao soi in the north
description: Coconut curry noodles with crisp noodles on top, pickled mustard greens and lime. Northern Thai, and barely known abroad.

title: Eat bun cha at lunchtime in Hanoi
description: Grilled pork patties in a bowl of sweet-sour broth with cold noodles and herbs. A lunch dish; the stalls close by two.

title: Eat com tam, broken rice with grilled pork
description: Rice grains broken in milling, once the cheap leftover and now a Saigon breakfast in its own right.

title: Grill your own Korean barbecue with the banchan
description: The side dishes come free and are refilled. Wrap the meat in lettuce with ssamjang and eat it in one bite.

title: Eat bibimbap in the city it comes from
description: Jeonju's version uses beef tartare and rice cooked in beef broth. Mix it thoroughly; not mixing it is the mistake.

title: Eat a Sichuan hotpot and learn what ma la means
description: Numbing peppercorn as well as chilli heat. Order a split pot if you want to be able to taste anything afterwards.

title: Take yum cha slowly on a Sunday morning
description: Tea first, then trolleys. Tap two fingers on the table when someone pours for you; it means thank you.

title: Eat roujiamo and biangbiang noodles in the Muslim Quarter
description: A pork or beef flatbread sandwich claimed as the world's oldest, and a noodle whose character has 58 strokes.

title: Eat chaat in Old Delhi
description: Sweet, sour, hot and crunchy at once. Go where there is a queue and where the water is bottled.

title: Eat a South Indian thali off a banana leaf
description: Endless refills of rice, sambar, rasam and curd, eaten with the right hand. Fold the leaf towards you when you finish.

title: Eat Amritsari kulcha with chole
description: Stuffed bread baked in a tandoor until blistered, crushed with butter, and eaten with chickpeas at a roadside dhaba.

title: Eat assam laksa at a Penang hawker stall
description: Sour tamarind and mackerel broth with thick rice noodles, mint and pineapple. Nothing like the coconut laksa elsewhere.

title: Eat chilli crab with mantou to mop it up
description: Invented in Singapore in the 1950s. Order the fried buns; the sauce is the point and you will want to finish it.

title: Eat gudeg for breakfast in Yogyakarta
description: Young jackfruit stewed for hours in palm sugar and coconut until it goes mahogany. Sweet, and eaten first thing.

title: Eat Cebu lechon carved off the spit
description: Roasted whole over charcoal, stuffed with lemongrass and needing no sauce, which is the Cebuano boast.

title: Eat rice and curry with five or six sides
description: The everyday meal: rice, a curry, a mallum, a sambol and a papadam, mixed with your fingers on the plate.

title: Eat momos with tomato achar
description: Steamed or fried dumplings from the Newar kitchens of the valley, with a roasted tomato and sesame dip.

title: Eat plov cooked in a kazan the size of a table
description: Rice, lamb, carrot and whole garlic, cooked in the morning and sold until it runs out. Every city cooks it differently.

title: Eat khuushuur and drink suutei tsai
description: Fried mutton pastries and salted milk tea. Refusing the tea in a ger is worse manners than not finishing it.

title: Work through a Taipei night market
description: Oyster omelette, beef noodle soup, pepper buns. Stinky tofu is the test; the smell is far worse than the taste.

title: Eat fish amok steamed in a banana leaf
description: Freshwater fish in coconut and kroeung curry paste, steamed rather than boiled, which is what makes it Khmer.

title: Eat mohinga for breakfast
description: Catfish and banana-stem soup with rice noodles, sold from pavement stalls before seven. The national breakfast.

title: Eat ema datshi and mean it
description: Whole chillies stewed in yak cheese. Chilli is the vegetable here, not the seasoning, and the national dish is unapologetic.

title: Eat a full mezze until the table runs out of room
description: Twenty small plates before anything grilled arrives. Order less than you think and it will still be too much.

title: Eat hummus at a dedicated hummusia at breakfast
description: Warm, with olive oil, chickpeas and pita, eaten in the morning at a place that sells nothing else and closes by two.

title: Eat mansaf, and eat it with your right hand
description: Lamb cooked in fermented dried yoghurt over rice and flatbread. The national dish, and a communal one.

title: Eat baklava where it is taken most seriously
description: Forty layers, Antep pistachios, protected by origin. The city has a UNESCO listing for its cooking.

title: Eat machboos and luqaimat at an Emirati table
description: Spiced rice with meat, then dumplings in date syrup. Emirati food is surprisingly hard to find in Dubai unless you look.

title: Eat tacos al pastor cut off the trompo
description: Lebanese shawarma technique on pork with pineapple, brought by immigrants to Puebla in the 1930s. Two small tortillas, always.

title: Eat mole negro in Oaxaca
description: More than thirty ingredients including chocolate and several chillies, cooked over a day. Oaxaca claims seven distinct moles.

title: Eat gumbo and beignets on the same day
description: A roux the colour of a copper penny, and square doughnuts under an unreasonable quantity of icing sugar at Cafe du Monde.

title: Queue for Central Texas brisket at opening
description: Post oak, salt and pepper, twelve hours, no sauce. The good places sell out by early afternoon and the queue starts before opening.

title: Eat a slice folded, standing at the counter
description: Thin, wide, foldable, sold by the slice. The dollar slice is mostly gone but the fold is not negotiable.

title: Eat poutine after midnight
description: Chips, gravy and cheese curds that must squeak. If they do not squeak they are not fresh enough.

title: Eat a Montreal bagel straight from the wood oven
description: Boiled in honey water and baked over wood. Smaller, sweeter and denser than the New York kind, and open all night.

title: Eat jerk pork from a drum pan at Boston Bay
description: Where jerk was commercialised, cooked over pimento wood in a split oil drum. Scotch bonnet, allspice and smoke.

title: Order coffee the way Melbourne taught the world
description: The flat white, the magic and a serious argument about roasts. Italian and Greek migration built this, not a chain.

title: Eat a hangi cooked in the ground
description: Meat and vegetables steamed in an earth oven for hours. In Rotorua some are cooked using geothermal steam instead of hot rocks.
